It also happens this way to the person when they have defended themselves against sins and have overcome them; then the small dogs come, which the person does not think to guard against. These are companions, or society, or trinkets, or the pastimes of people, and the kindness of people. These tear at them here and there, and tug at their heart and their inner being, so that of necessity they must rot in all divine life and in divine earnestness, and they do not feel God's grace and devotion. This small temptation is often much more harmful to the person than the great trials; for the person guards against the latter with diligence and considers them to be wrong; but the person does not want to pay attention to these small defects, nor consider them wrong. In the same way that all things that are not recognized are much more harmful than those that are recognized, so too is this danger, which one does not regard or heed much, such as companionship, society, or pleasure in creatures. Now, just as the deer is heated by every hunt, and its thirst increases all the more because of it, so should the person be heated more by every temptation toward divine love for our Lord, and be incited or pressed by every trial in true thirst to run more and more into God, where they find nothing but truth, joy, righteousness, and comfort. <note>Note from the 1543 edition.</note>

Now the hunters sometimes do this: when the deer is too tired and too parched, they feed the dogs a little, and these are thus held back. When they are sure of the deer in the game park, they let the deer wander a little so that it is somewhat strengthened thereby, so that it may then better endure the hunt. Our Lord also does this to the person when He sees that the hunt is becoming too much for them and the trial too great; He holds them back a little, and then a drop falls into the mouth of the person's heart—that is, a sweet taste of the sweetness of divine things. These strengthen them so much that all things that are not God taste bitter and repulsive <note>original: "widerzehme" [contrary/repulsive]</note> to them, and then it seems to them that they have entirely overcome all their distress.

<summary>Johannes Tauler uses the metaphor of a deer hunt to explain how small, unrecognized distractions can rot a person's spiritual life more than major sins. He describes how God provides moments of divine sweetness to strengthen the soul during periods of intense spiritual trial.</summary>
<keywords>temptation, divine love, spiritual trials, distractions, deer metaphor, grace, Johannes Tauler, 16th century sermons</keywords>

He would have to wish him well, grant him good, desire it for him, and also do the very best for that same person, if he were able to take and receive it. To summarize everything that has been discussed so far, it is first necessary to remind the reader: that the concern here is not the origin of experience, but rather what lies within it. The former belongs to empirical psychology, and even there it could never be properly developed without the latter, which belongs to the critique of knowledge and specifically of the understanding.

Experience consists of intuitions <note>original: "Anschauungen"</note>, which belong to sensibility, and of judgments, which are solely a task of the understanding. However, those judgments which the understanding makes solely from sensible intuitions are still far from being judgments of experience <note>original: "Erfahrungsurtheile"</note>. In the first case, the judgment would only connect the perceptions just as they are given in sensible intuition; in the latter case, however, the judgments are meant to state what experience contains in general, and thus not what is contained in mere perception, the validity of which is merely subjective. The judgment of experience must therefore add something to the sensible intuition and its logical connection (after it has been made general through comparison) in a judgment; something which determines the synthetic judgment as necessary and thereby as universally valid. This can be nothing other than that concept which represents the intuition as determined in itself in respect to one form of judgment rather than another, as

<summary>Kant distinguishes between mere perception and judgments of experience, explaining that the latter require the addition of universal concepts from the understanding to achieve objective validity. He clarifies that his investigation focuses on the logical structure of experience rather than its psychological origin.</summary>
<keywords>experience, understanding, intuition, judgment of experience, perception, synthetic judgment, empirical psychology, universal validity</keywords>

One can even notice this distinction in the assessment of health. To anyone who possesses it, health is immediately pleasant <note>at least negatively, as the absence of all bodily pain</note>. However, in order to say that it is **good**, one must further direct it through reason toward purposes, namely that it is a state that makes us fit for all our business. Regarding <term>happiness</term> <note>original: "Glückseligkeit"</note> <margin>a</margin>, everyone finally believes they can call the greatest sum <note>both in quantity and duration</note> of the pleasantries of life a true, and indeed the highest, good. Yet reason also rebels against this. Agreeableness is <term>enjoyment</term> <note>original: "Genuß"</note>. But if life is aimed at this alone, it would be foolish to be scrupulous regarding the means that procure it for us, whether it were obtained passively, from the generosity of nature, or through self-activity and our own labor. But reason will never be convinced that the existence of a human being has a value <margin>b</margin> in itself when they live merely to enjoy <note>even if they are extremely busy in this regard</note>, even if they were to best serve as a means for others who are also only out for enjoyment, and did so because they shared in all pleasure through sympathy. Only through what he does without regard for enjoyment, in full freedom and independently of what nature could provide for him even passively, does he give his existence, as the existence of a person, an absolute <margin>c</margin> value; and happiness, with the full abundance of its pleasantness, is by no means an unconditional good.*

***

* An obligation to enjoy is a manifest absurdity. The same must therefore also apply to a supposed obligation to all actions that have enjoyment as their only goal; regardless of how spiritually conceived <note>or refined</note> this enjoyment may be, even if it were a mystical, so-called heavenly enjoyment.

### *On the proportionality of the limbs.* Chap. CLXXV.

All the parts of any animal must be corresponding to its whole: that is, a creature that is short and thick must have every limb in itself short and thick; one that is long and slender should have long and slender limbs; and the mediocre <note>In this context, mediocre refers to a middle or average build.</note> should have limbs of that same mediocrity. I intend for the same to be said of plants which have not been maimed by man or by winds, because these put forth youth over old age, and thus their natural proportionality is destroyed.

### *On the joint of the hands with the arm.* Chap. CLXXVI.

The joint of the arm with its hand decreases when gripping, and thickens when the hand is opened; and the arm between the elbow and the hand does the opposite from every direction. This arises because in opening the hand, the internal muscles <note>original: "muscoli domestici," referring to the flexor muscles on the inner side of the forearm</note> extend and make the arm thinner between the elbow and the hand; and when the hand is clenched, the internal and external muscles <note>original: "muscoli domestici e siluestri," where "silvestri" refers to the extensor muscles on the outer side of the forearm</note> withdraw and thicken, but the external muscles alone move away from the bone because they are pulled by the bending of the hand.
